# Industrial Services Unit — Turnaround or Exit
## Assessment, Decision Rule, and Twelve-Month Plan

**Version 2.0 — for board decision at this meeting.**
Circulation: Board; Group CEO; Group CFO; Chair of Audit; unit Managing Director and CFO; Group General Counsel. Shared-customer sections (§3.5, §8.4) are circulated to the two divisional presidents **after** the board has fixed the adjudication rule at §3.5, not before — the reason is set out there and is not a matter of trust. Disclosure beyond this list is governed by §6.6 and by no other authority.

Evidence key: **[F]** fact supplied or verified · **[A]** assumption authored here for illustration only · **[H]** hypothesis with a named test · **[J]** practitioner judgement. Annex A explains the key; Annex B holds every illustrative number in one place so that none of them can be mistaken for evidence when read in isolation.

**No financials were supplied with the brief.** Accordingly this document contains no financial findings. Every threshold below is expressed as a ratio, a rank or a sign test, so that it survives re-basing onto the actuals in Week 1. Where an absolute figure appears in the body it carries **[A]** and exists only to show the shape of the arithmetic.

---

## 0. Decision on a page

**Recommendation.** Stop treating this as turnaround-versus-exit. The likeliest right answer, on the pattern the brief itself describes, is **partial exit: contract to a defensible core, and dispose of or close the remainder** [H]. Run two tracks — *Fix-and-Prove* and *Exit-Ready* — from Day 0 under one owner and one budget, with exit preparation beginning immediately rather than at the end, because a decision to sell taken in Month 10 with no vendor diligence behind it is not an option, only a wish. Pre-commit the switching rule now, at §7, while no one's position is yet attached to an answer.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Headline** | Dual-track from Day 0; **soft gate Month 6, binding gate Month 9**; Month 12 deliverable is *a decision plus a live, executed process* — not a closed transaction (§6.5) |
| Diagnosis, provisional | **Mixed and asymmetric** [H]. The structural share is expected to be concentrated in identifiable segments rather than spread across the unit; that is why "the unit" is the wrong unit of analysis (§3, §4) |
| Primary diagnostic artifact | **Three-year EBIT bridge** — volume, price, mix, input inflation, productivity, cost-out actually landed, one-offs — plus a parallel **cash bridge**. Three weeks from existing ledgers. Nothing else is commissioned until these exist (§3.1) |
| Why two cost programmes did not work | Most probable [H]: a mix-and-price problem was treated as a cost problem, and the second round removed capacity that carried gross profit. The bridge settles it; §3.2 states the interpretive rule rather than an answer |
| The number no one has | A **group-level customer P&L**. Where this unit serves customers of profitable divisions, the price concession that protects the group relationship is very often booked entirely here [H]. Until that view exists the board does not know what this unit loses (§3.5) |
| Sector-specific killers, screened explicitly | Customer insourcing · OEM service-arm encroachment · loss of prequalification, licence or approved-vendor status · deteriorating HSE record (§3.4, Tests 6–9) |
| Where profit is most likely to survive | Recurring, compliance-mandated, outage-critical and emergency work, in geographies above the density breakpoint, with a certification or embedded-access moat (§4) |
| Where losses are most likely to sit | Fixed-price multi-year contracts without cost indexation · branches below density threshold · competitively bid general manning · possibly the three largest customers by revenue (§4.3) |
| Principal risk | **Not the market — the bench.** Best managers are already leaving. A unit that cannot staff a turnaround cannot execute one, and a buyer prices thin management directly. Fixable in 30 days and by the board alone (§6.2) |
| Decision rule | **Four kill conditions** (any one fails → exit primary, automatically) and **five scored conditions** (§7). No new business case required to switch |
| Exit alternatives | **Five, ranked**, with partial exit first (§5) |
| Value test | **Net exit value** (full formula, §8.1) compared against **NPV of continuing** including the cash cost of funding further losses and the option value of the turnaround (§8.2). Neither number means anything alone |
| Cost of the plan | Diagnostic and data build · retention · exit readiness · contract exit and closure provisions. Structure at §6.7; illustrative magnitudes in Annex B |
| Decisions sought | **Four**, §1, at this meeting |

### 0.1 Before anything else: the six manoeuvres that will destroy both outcomes

An organisation told it has one year to produce a profitability number will produce a profitability number. There are six well-worn ways to do that in four quarters which permanently destroy the turnaround *and* the sale value, and each is discovered in diligence:

1. Deferring maintenance and fleet capex.
2. Harvesting the backlog on price — booking volume below contribution to fill the order book.
3. Releasing contract provisions and warranty reserves.
4. Cutting the bid, estimating and technical-authority teams (the second restructuring may already have done this).
5. Stretching payables and squeezing subcontractors, i.e. borrowing from the supply chain that delivers the work.
6. Under-recognising loss-making contract positions and over-recognising unbilled work in progress.

**Board action requested:** each of these six is placed on a monthly one-page exception report to the Audit Chair, with the unit CFO personally attesting. This is not distrust of the unit's leadership; it is the removal of a temptation that the deadline itself creates, and saying so plainly is kinder than leaving people to be judged later for responding rationally to the incentive we set.

---

## 1. The four decisions requested at this meeting

| # | Decision | Why now |
|---|---|---|
| **D1** | **Re-specify the deadline** as a *decision* deadline with an evidence standard, not a *profitability* deadline. Month 12 requires: a proven fully-loaded contribution core, a validated run-rate trajectory, and an exit process capable of signature — not a break-even quarter | Without this, §0.1 happens by default (§2) |
| **D2** | **Appoint one accountable owner** with full P&L authority over the unit, reporting to the Group CEO, with the three-branch incentive at §6.1 approved in the same motion | Every week of dual reporting costs a departure (§6.2) |
| **D3** | **Authorise the dual track and the Day-0 start of exit readiness** — vendor diligence, carve-out P&L, standalone cost model, data room — and approve the disclosure architecture at §6.6 | The calendar, not the analysis, is what kills the exit option (§6.5) |
| **D4** | **Adopt the switching rule at §7 as pre-committed**, and name the Group CFO as adjudicator of the shared-customer economics at §3.5 | Rules agreed before the answer is known are the only rules that hold once it is |

Retention actions at §6.2 need no board decision beyond D2's budget line and should be executed within 30 days of this meeting.

---

## 2. On the instruction as given

The board's words were "one final year to produce a credible path to profitability or exit." Two readings sit inside that sentence and they lead to different companies.

**Reading A — profitability deadline.** The unit must show a better EBIT number by Month 12. Achievable, and achievable dishonestly (§0.1).

**Reading B — decision deadline with an evidence standard.** By Month 12 the board must be able to state, on evidence, which of the five options at §5 it is taking, and be far enough into execution that the option is real.

Reading B is what a board can actually act on, and it is also the reading a buyer, a lender and an auditor will each independently apply. The plan below is built on B. If the board prefers A, the plan still runs — but the exception report at §0.1 becomes the single most important document the Audit Chair receives, and the exit route should be assumed to be worth materially less.

---

## 3. Diagnosis: structural or execution-driven

### 3.1 The primary artifact — a three-year EBIT bridge, and a cash bridge beside it

Nothing else is commissioned until these two exist. Both are buildable in two to three weeks from ledgers the unit already has, and together they answer the board's first question more directly than any interview programme.

**EBIT bridge, Year 0 → Year 3, decomposed into:**

| Component | What a large adverse value means |
|---|---|
| Volume | Demand or share loss — read with Test 8 (win-rate/churn) before calling it structural |
| **Price realisation** | Structural if it appears across all segments; execution if concentrated in particular contracts, years or estimators |
| **Mix** | Structural — the profitable work is shrinking faster than the unprofitable work. This is the single most commonly missed driver |
| Input cost inflation not recovered | Structural if contract form prevents recovery (Test 5); execution if indexation clauses exist and were never invoked |
| Productivity / field utilisation | Execution — and the most tractable line in the bridge |
| **Cost-out actually landed in the run rate** | If the landed figure is materially below the programme's claimed figure, the failure was governance, not strategy |
| One-offs, provisions, contract-position remeasurements | Isolate before any conclusion. Restructuring charges and provision movements routinely mask the underlying trend in both directions |

**Cash bridge, same three years.** For a loss-making industrial-services business the cash view is not a supplement; it is half the decision. A unit losing $X of EBIT may be absorbing $2X of cash or may be cash-neutral, and those are two different boards' patience levels and two different sale prices. Required lines: unbilled work in progress and contract assets by ageing · retentions receivable and their realisability · claims and variations recognised but not agreed with the customer · loss-making contract provisions and their adequacy · maintenance versus growth capex, split · working capital days by service line · intercompany funding drawn.

**Sign test, applied at Week 3.** If EBIT losses are stable but cash absorption is worsening, the reported P&L is flattering and the runway is shorter than the board believes. That single finding, if it appears, moves the exit track to primary immediately and is a kill condition at §7.

### 3.2 Reconstructing the two cost programmes — the interpretive rule, not an answer

The temptation is to infer contribution lost from the fact that EBIT did not move. That inference is circular: if losses are flat, contribution lost *must* equal cost removed by arithmetic, and the resulting "decremental margin" is a restatement of the assumption, not a finding. Worse, it is defeated by its own alternatives — price erosion or unrecovered inflation of similar magnitude would produce exactly the same flat EBIT while the departed revenue carried little contribution at all.

So it must be measured bottom-up, and only after the bridge has isolated price and inflation:

**Measure:** for the revenue that actually left over the period, the fully-loaded contribution those specific contracts and branches were generating in the year before exit. Then compare with cost genuinely removed from the run rate (not announced).

| Contribution lost ÷ cost removed | Reading | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| **Under ~25%** | The cuts were largely genuine overhead. The cost base was fat and is now less so | The loss is then explained by price, mix or inflation. Structural — go to §4 segmentation immediately |
| **~25–45%** | Mixed. Some overhead, some capacity | Both tracks live; scrutinise which capabilities went |
| **Above ~45%** | The cuts removed revenue-generating capacity — supervision, estimating, technical authority, field productivity roles | The unit did not have a cost problem and now has a capability problem it did not have three years ago. **A third cost programme would complete the process.** Rebuild before any exit process, or sell a declining asset at a declining multiple |

Then the qualitative half, which is quick and decisive: list the roles removed. If they were disproportionately supervisors, estimators, technical authorities and planners, the answer above is already known.

### 3.3 The honest signal already in front of the board

Best managers transferring out is not merely a symptom; it is an internal forecast produced by the people with the best information and no incentive to flatter it [J]. It should be read as data about the unit's prospects and, separately, as the binding constraint on any turnaround. Both readings point at §6.2.

### 3.4 Nine tests, thirty days

| # | Test | Method | Structural if… | Execution if… |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Margin dispersion** | Fully-loaded contribution by contract, ranked, comparing like work | Whole distribution under water; best quartile barely breaks even | Wide dispersion on comparable work — someone in the unit already knows how to do this profitably |
| 2 | **Price vs. input index** | Realised price per unit of work, five years, against labour and materials indices | Price tracks below input inflation in every segment | Lag concentrated in specific contracts, years or signatories |
| 3 | **Bid-to-final variance** | Bid margin vs. as-built, by contract, estimator, service line | Variance small; bids were always thin — market price is below cost | Variance large and negative — work won by under-estimating. Fixable, and quickly |
| 4 | **Density economics** | Contribution vs. technician/asset density per geography; locate the breakpoint | No geography clears the threshold | Clear breakpoint with a definable subset above it — **this is the shape of a keepable business** |
| 5 | **Contract form audit** | Every contract above a materiality threshold: fixed vs. cost-plus, indexation, change-order mechanism, term, termination, liability caps, LDs | Losses concentrate in a form the market now demands and the unit cannot price safely | Losses concentrate where change-order and indexation rights exist but are unused; unbilled variations un-pursued |
| 6 | **Prequalification and licence integrity** | Approved-vendor status, certifications, licences, safety qualification scores, per customer and per statutory regime; three-year trend | Status lost for reasons not recoverable (scale, financial-standing tests, insurance capacity) | Status lapsed through administrative neglect — recoverable, and cheaply |
| 7 | **HSE record and trend** | TRIR/LTIFR trend, serious-incident frequency, near-miss reporting rate, regulator interactions, customer audit outcomes | Sector risk profile has shifted beyond the unit's insurable or operable capability | Deterioration tracks the loss of supervisors — a capability symptom, and the fastest-moving destroyer of both order book and exit value |
| 8 | **Win-rate and churn decomposition** | Win rate by bid type and year; renewal rate on recurring contracts; every loss coded: price, capability, delivery failure, prequalification failure, **customer insourcing**, **OEM service-arm encroachment**, customer capex cycle | Losses cluster on insourcing, OEM encroachment or capex cycle — the addressable market is contracting | Losses cluster on price errors, delivery failures or bids not submitted |
| 9 | **Relative cost position** | Cost per productive field hour, overhead as % of direct cost, fleet utilisation, benchmarked against listed comparators and known regional competitors | The unit is structurally 15%+ above best comparable cost at equivalent scale, with no path to scale | Gap is in overhead layers, utilisation or subcontract leakage |

**Two further screens, run in parallel, t…[truncated]

# Global Employee Empowerment & Adaptive Culture Initiative
## Guidance on Regional Leadership Adaptation — Recommendation for Sponsor Group

**Version 2.0 — complete. Prepared for sponsor group decision, and for prior circulation to the fourteen regional people leads. Not yet for employee communication.**

---

### How we would ask you to use this

One note only, and then the substance.

This version differs from v1.0 in three ways that the reviewers were right to insist on. It now asks for specific decisions, with money and a date attached (§12). It answers the questions the first draft deferred — most importantly what the centre itself is bound by (§9). And the regional material has been re-cut so that no colleague opens it and finds their country described inside someone else's card.

The regional cards in §6 remain what they were: **working hypotheses, offered so that they can be corrected**. Where a region has its own diagnostic data, that data replaces the card and the card is retired for that unit (§5.4). A card returned to us unamended will be read not as agreement but as a sign that the conversation has not yet taken place, and we would come back for it.

Two courtesies we would ask the sponsor group to extend before this travels further. First, that the fourteen regional people leads and the four regional MDs see §§3, 4 and 9 and have time to respond in their own way before the board pack is assembled — a programme about devolved authority that arrives in a region fully formed has already contradicted itself, and colleagues will notice that before they notice anything else. Second, that §10 (consultation and legal gates) be walked through with Group Legal, the European Works Council secretariat and Group Reward before any part of this is described to employees anywhere. The likeliest single cause of avoidable damage is a well-intentioned announcement that reaches a works council after it reaches a newspaper, or reaches an employee before it reaches their own supervisor.

---

## 1. Recommendation on a page

**Adopt a thin global core and a wide local expression: four employee entitlements defined centrally as *floors*, with a formal alternative-form process where a floor cannot lawfully or structurally be met; delivery method, language, sequencing and naming devolved entirely to regions; four instrumented pilots in Year 1 with a common measurement spine but deliberately different local design; and a published protocol binding the centre to the same discipline it asks of others.**

| | |
|---|---|
| Global mandate | **Four entitlements only** (§3) — decision rights at the lowest competent level; an answered route for dissent; tolerance of good-faith error; employee-initiated internal movement. Each stated as a floor, each with a named-approver alternative-form route (§3.6) |
| Devolved to regions | Language, ritual, sequencing, symbolism, manager incentives, pace, communication channels, and the programme's name. We would suggest the centre resist standardising even the name |
| Year 1 shape | **Four pilots — one high-authority-distance, one low, one deskless-majority, one recently-acquired entity** — different in design, identical in instrumentation (§7) |
| Principal risk | Middle-manager status and grade loss, not employee resistance (§8) |
| The centre's own obligation | **Published reversal protocol**: the centre may reverse a devolved decision, but must give written reasons to the same audience that saw the decision, and reversal counts are reported quarterly beside regional metrics (§9) |
| Measurement | Within-region trend on four behavioural proxies weighted 70%, survey items 30%; acquiescence correction applied before any cross-region view is shown (§8.3) |
| Numeric failure test | Empowerment survey index +5 points or more while decision latency on the instrumented decision class improves <10% and internal-move rate is flat = declared failure, programme paused, no further capital (§8.5) |
| Investment sought | **$14.2M Year 1, $10.6M Year 2** (illustrative, assumptions in §12.1), of which $6.9M is manager time relief — the line most often omitted and most often fatal |
| Funding split | Central P&L funds diagnostic, instrumentation, platform, central team and pilot facilitation; regions fund manager time with a **60% central offset in Y1, 30% in Y2, nil thereafter** (§12.3) |
| Decisions requested | **Three** — §12.5, sought at the sponsor group meeting on **18 March** |
| Programme owner | Group Chief People Officer, sponsor; named programme director recruited internally within 30 days of approval |

### 1.1 The core proposition, and how confident we are in it

Empowerment mechanisms do not transfer between contexts; the conditions that make them work can be built in each. *(This is our considered assertion from practitioner experience, not a finding — see the evidence key at §14. We flag it because the sponsor group is entitled to know which of our statements are evidenced and which are judgement.)*

The specific failure we are trying to avoid is well documented in our own past programmes: exported behavioural vocabulary — "speak up", "own it", "disagree and commit" — produces regions that become fluent at the annual survey and unchanged on Tuesday morning. That outcome is worse than no initiative, because it consumes the credibility a second attempt would require.

---

## 2. Diagnosis before we design

### 2.1 The framing we would gently ask the sponsor group to test

The initiative is currently described as culture change. The evidence available to us may instead describe a **decision-rights and information-flow** problem wearing culture-change clothing. Only one of those two responds to leadership behaviour work, and we would rather establish which we have before committing eight figures to the wrong one.

| Candidate driver | What leadership/empowerment training does to it |
|---|---|
| Decision rights formally held too high | Nothing — requires delegation-of-authority redesign |
| Rights delegated on paper, retracted in practice | Nothing until retraction is made visible and costly (§9) |
| Information does not reach the level holding authority | **Amplifies harm** — confident decisions on poor data |
| Managers lack coaching capability | Improves, *if* paired with funded time relief (§8.4) |
| Reward and grading pay for control, not for developing others | Nothing — the incentive wins every time (§8.2) |
| Employees have voice but no evidence it is ever acted on | Worsens — a further unanswered invitation deepens cynicism |
| Working-language barrier suppresses contribution | Nothing — needs channel design, not confidence-building (§11.1) |

### 2.2 The diagnostic we propose

Five weeks, no design freeze until it reports: 60 structured conversations across four organisational levels in eight countries (including two deskless-majority sites); an audit of the documented delegation-of-authority matrix against actual practice in twelve units; and a language-barrier check in the four sites where the working language is not the local one. Cost **$310K**.

If it finds that decision rights are formally too high, the largest part of the Year 2 training envelope should be redirected to delegation architecture and the pilot scope revised before commitment. This is the cheapest consequential decision in the programme.

### 2.3 The uncomfortable question, now answered rather than deferred

Will headquarters be bound by the same four entitlements? If regional colleagues discover that the centre reserves the right to overturn devolved decisions without giving reasons, the initiative becomes rhetoric and everything downstream of it is wasted. v1.0 left this open. **§9 now answers it with a specific, testable, reportable mechanism**, and we would ask the sponsor group to adopt or amend it rather than to note it.

---

## 3. What is fixed everywhere: four entitlements, stated as floors

Framed as what an employee is entitled to, not as how a manager must behave, so that very different conduct can honour them.

### 3.1 Entitlement I — decision rights sit at the lowest competent level
**Floor:** every employee can name the classes of decision they own and point to a recent instance of exercising one without seeking permission. *Competent* is doing real work in that sentence; this is not an argument for uniform flat structures.

### 3.2 Entitlement II — there is a route for dissent, and it is answered
**Floor:** every employee has at least one available channel through which they can contradict a superior's view **and receive a response**. The channel may be a written pre-read, a skip-level, a facilitated small group, a mentor, a shift huddle, or an anonymous board. It need never be a raised hand in a large meeting. The answered part is the floor; the form is entirely local.

**Firewall, mandatory:** this channel is expressly **not** a statutory reporting channel. Disagreement about a business decision is not a protected disclosure. The two must be separately named, separately routed and separately governed, or we create legal exposure on one side and chill genuine reporting on the other (§10.3).

### 3.3 Entitlement III — good-faith error is absorbed, not attributed
**Floor:** within each unit, at least one specific, visible instance per quarter in which a good-faith mistake was absorbed rather than attributed, and the team can name it. Demonstrated, never announced. In several regions this must be framed collectively rather than individually to be usable at all (§6).

### 3.4 Entitlement IV — employees can initiate their own movement
**Floor (revised from v1.0):** an employee may apply for an internal role, project or rotation **without the incumbent manager holding a veto and without the manager being informed in advance of the application**.

v1.0 stated this as an absolute and was wrong to. In parts of the Gulf, mobility between entities is constrained by employer-tied work permits and is a legal matter, not a cultural one. In Japan, Korea and Taiwan, seniority-anchored career and reward structures make unrestricted lateral self-nomination structurally disruptive in ways that a global mandate cannot responsibly overrule from a distance. The floor above is the most we can hold everywhere; where even that cannot be met, §3.6 applies.

### 3.5 Everything else is regional property
Language, ceremony, sequencing, symbolism, tooling, incentives, cadence, and the programme's own name.

### 3.6 The alternative-form process (in place of exemption)

We deliberately avoid the word *exemption*, and avoid asking any region to refuse. A region that cannot meet a floor is asked instead to **propose the nearest form it can honour**, and to say what it would take to close the remainder.

| Element | Provision |
|---|---|
| Trigger | Legal impossibility, collective-agreement conflict, or structural impossibility (not difficulty, not discomfort) |
| Form | Two pages: which floor, why, the alternative mechanism proposed, and the condition under which the floor becomes reachable |
| Approver | **Group Chief People Officer**, countersigned by the Regional MD and by Group Legal |
| Duration | **12 months maximum**, renewable once with fresh reasoning |
| Visibility | Entered in an internally published register, reviewed quarterly by the sponsor group |
| Presumption | An alternative form is accepted unless it is materially weaker than the floor. We expect four to eight across the network in Year 1 and would be suspicious of zero |

---

## 4. The adaptation logic

### 4.1 Four variables, rather than a general culture model

We would ask each region to place itself on four axes only, because these four determine whether a given mechanism functions or backfires.

| Axis | The question | What it changes |
|---|---|---|
| **Authority basis** | Does a manager's authority derive from role or from demonstrated expertise? | Whether devolution reads as trust or as abandonment |
| **Directness of disagreement** | Can dissent be public without cost to either party? | The design of the dissent channel (Entitlement II) |
| **Attribution of error** | Does a mistake attach to a person, a team, or a system? | Whether error tolerance can be individual or must be collective (III) |
| **Ambiguity tolerance** | Is an open brief experienced as freedom, or as information withheld? | How much structure must accompany autonomy |

### 4.2 The working rule

> High authority distance and low disagreement-directness do not mean empowerment is unwelcome. They mean it must be **granted rather than seized** — granted visibly, specifically, bounded, and by someone whose authority the team already accepts.

In such contexts an open invitation ("bring me your ideas") is not empowerment; it is a test most colleagues will decline to sit. The functioning equivalent is a named, bounded, publicly conferred mandate: *"Priya decides this class of exception up to this threshold. She does not need to ask me. If you disagree with her, take it to her."* Our practitioner judgement is that this single act moves more behaviour than a quarter of workshops — offered as judgement, not as measured finding (§14), and testable inside the pilots via the decision-latency proxy.

### 4.3 Sponsorship: a default with a visible opt-out

**Default:** regional sponsors are selected on observed practice — leaders whose own teams already exhibit the four entitlements — rather than on rank.

We acknowledged in v1.0 that this backfires in several regions, then handed the choice back, which was no recommendation at all. The corrected position: the default stands, and a region wishing to depart from it does so through a **one-page note countersigned by the Regional MD and the programme director**, logged in the same register as §3.6. Departures are expected and unremarkable; what matters is that they are visible.

Where the practitioner sponsor sits two or three levels below the Regional MD, the workable form is almost always a **pair** — the senior figure as visible patron providing cover and air, the practitioner as the working engine. A junior sponsor without a senior patron will in several regions be read, reasonably, as the centre not taking the region seriously.

---

## 5. Using the regional cards well

### 5.1 What they are
Starting hypotheses about context, to be returned marked up within 45 days. They describe patterns we have observed in workplaces, not peoples.

### 5.2 What each card contains
Working hypothesis on the four axes · where the gap likely sits · behaviour to add · behaviour to drop · failure mode · **leading indicator observable by day 60** · legal or structural watch item.

### 5.3 The 60-day indicator, and why it is on every card
The failure modes that matter most — courteous non-adoption, affirmative response with no movement — are precisely the ones you cannot detect by asking. Each card therefore names an observable proxy visible within 60 days.

### 5.4 The supersession rule
**Where unit-level diagnostic data exists, it supersedes the card, and the card is retired for that unit.** Within-country variance in work values routinely exceeds between-country variance; function, site history and acquisition lineage frequently dominate nationality. This applies to every card, not only where we have noted it.

### 5.5 Scope note
Cards cover the fourteen clusters where we have wholly-owned or majority-controlled operations. Russia and Belarus are **out of scope** for this programme pending the Group's standing position on those entities; the programme director should not open a workstream there without a written instruction from the sponsor group.

---

## 6. Regional cards

### Card A — Anglosphere (US, Canada, UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand)

| | |
|---|---|
| Working hypothesis | Low authority distance; direct disagreement acceptable; individual error attribution; moderate-to-high ambiguity tolerance |
| Likely gap | Not permission — **follow-through**. Voice is already loud; evidence that it changes anything is thin |
| Add | Visible closure loops: "here is what we did with what you told us, here is what we declined, and why" |
| Drop | Announcing empowerment. The region has heard it and discounts it |
| Failure mode | Ironic compliance; strong survey movement, unchanged decision latency |
| 60-day indicator | Ratio of raised items with a documented, dated response — target 80%+; skip-level uptake |
| Watch item | Strong individual error attribution and litigation exposure make Entitlement III hard: blame follows the name. US at-will/discipline documentation practice cuts against visible error absorption |
| Internal variance not to flatten | UK indirectness is closer to the Nordic-plus-hedging pattern than to US directness; Quebec sits closer to Card C than to the rest of Canada; the Australian register tolerates challenge to authority that would be career-limiting in the US |

### Card B — Germanic & Nordic (DE, AT, CH, NL, SE, DK, NO, FI)

The board must be told plainly that the Month-12 deliverable is *a decision plus an executed process*, not a completed transaction — and therefore that vendor due diligence, the carve-out P&L, the standalone cost model and the data room must begin at **Month 0**, not Month 10, or the option is destroyed by the calendar. The document implies this and never sequences it.

**4. "Two of four conditions missed" is arbitrary and mis-specified.** It treats necessary conditions and progress conditions as interchangeable. Restructure as: **kill conditions** (any single failure → exit primary; e.g., no identifiable segment achieving positive fully-loaded contribution at scale) versus **scored conditions** (run-rate trajectory, cash, bid win-rate, retention of the top 30).

**5. "Paid on both outcomes symmetrically" is under-designed.** Symmetric pay does not neutralise asymmetric personal consequences. Specify the metric on each branch (verified run-rate EBIT and cash on one; net exit value against a pre-agreed floor on the other), and specify the third outcome — neither works, orderly closure — which currently carries no incentive at all and is therefore the outcome the owner will avoid longest.

**6. Net exit value is missing terms.** Add tax (loss carryforwards, disposal crystallisation), pension settlement, delivered working capital (frequently the largest cash line in a services deal), deferred/earn-out risk, and the retained-liability tail. More importantly, the formula has no denominator: net exit value is meaningless except against the NPV of continuing, including the cash cost of funding two further years of losses and the option value of the turnaround. State the comparison explicitly.

**7. The conflict of interest in the shared-customer analysis is unaddressed.** The document circulates the draft to the two divisional presidents whose customers overlap and then relies on their cooperation to build the group customer P&L. Those presidents have a direct interest in (a) understating the subsidy they receive and (b) overstating the group revenue at risk on divestment. Both claims must be independently tested — historically, cross-sell loss on divestment is far smaller than incumbent divisions forecast. Name it, and name who adjudicates.

**8. Accounting and financing consequences absent.** IFRS 5 held-for-sale classification, impairment triggers, discontinued-operations presentation and covenant impact all interact directly with the timing of the dual-track announcement. This is a live board decision and is not mentioned once.

**9. The binary framing is wrong, and the document's own logic says so.** §1 and §3 point toward a profitable density core surrounded by loss-making sub-scale branches and adverse fixed-price contracts. The likeliest right answer is therefore neither "turnaround" nor "exit" but **partial exit**: shrink to the defensible core, sell or close the remainder, and judge the residual on standalone economics. That option must sit at the top of the option set, not be buried in a seven-item list.

## E. Style

The document has imported wholesale the register of an unrelated prior deliverable — "How we would ask you to use this," "Two notes, then the substance," the [J]/[H] evidence key, "we would gently ask the board to test its own framing." The evidence key is a genuine improvement and should stay. The deference should not. Addressed to a board confronting a third consecutive loss year and a hard deadline, extended throat-clearing before the first substantive line reads as evasion. Invert the ratio: recommendation, decision rule, and the six-manoeuvres warning first; methodological caveats to an annex. # Industrial Services Unit — Turnaround or Exit
## Assessment, Decision Rule, and Twelve-Month Plan

**Version 2.0 — for board decision at this meeting.**
Circulation: Board; Group CEO; Group CFO; Chair of Audit; unit Managing Director and CFO; Group General Counsel. Shared-customer sections (§3.5, §8.4) are circulated to the two divisional presidents **after** the board has fixed the adjudication rule at §3.5, not before — the reason is set out there and is not a matter of trust. Disclosure beyond this list is governed by §6.6 and by no other authority.

Evidence key: **[F]** fact supplied or verified · **[A]** assumption authored here for illustration only · **[H]** hypothesis with a named test · **[J]** practitioner judgement. Annex A explains the key; Annex B holds every illustrative number in one place so that none of them can be mistaken for evidence when read in isolation.

**No financials were supplied with the brief.** Accordingly this document contains no financial findings. Every threshold below is expressed as a ratio, a rank or a sign test, so that it survives re-basing onto the actuals in Week 1. Where an absolute figure appears in the body it carries **[A]** and exists only to show the shape of the arithmetic.

---

## 0. Decision on a page

**Recommendation.** Stop treating this as turnaround-versus-exit. The likeliest right answer, on the pattern the brief itself describes, is **partial exit: contract to a defensible core, and dispose of or close the remainder** [H]. Run two tracks — *Fix-and-Prove* and *Exit-Ready* — from Day 0 under one owner and one budget, with exit preparation beginning immediately rather than at the end, because a decision to sell taken in Month 10 with no vendor diligence behind it is not an option, only a wish. Pre-commit the switching rule now, at §7, while no one's position is yet attached to an answer.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Headline** | Dual-track from Day 0; **soft gate Month 6, binding gate Month 9**; Month 12 deliverable is *a decision plus a live, executed process* — not a closed transaction (§6.5) |
| Diagnosis, provisional | **Mixed and asymmetric** [H]. The structural share is expected to be concentrated in identifiable segments rather than spread across the unit; that is why "the unit" is the wrong unit of analysis (§3, §4) |
| Primary diagnostic artifact | **Three-year EBIT bridge** — volume, price, mix, input inflation, productivity, cost-out actually landed, one-offs — plus a parallel **cash bridge**. Three weeks from existing ledgers. Nothing else is commissioned until these exist (§3.1) |
| Why two cost programmes did not work | Most probable [H]: a mix-and-price problem was treated as a cost problem, and the second round removed capacity that carried gross profit. The bridge settles it; §3.2 states the interpretive rule rather than an answer |
| The number no one has | A **group-level customer P&L**. Where this unit serves customers of profitable divisions, the price concession that protects the group relationship is very often booked entirely here [H]. Until that view exists the board does not know what this unit loses (§3.5) |
| Sector-specific killers, screened explicitly | Customer insourcing · OEM service-arm encroachment · loss of prequalification, licence or approved-vendor status · deteriorating HSE record (§3.4, Tests 6–9) |
| Where profit is most likely to survive | Recurring, compliance-mandated, outage-critical and emergency work, in geographies above the density breakpoint, with a certification or embedded-access moat (§4) |
| Where losses are most likely to sit | Fixed-price multi-year contracts without cost indexation · branches below density threshold · competitively bid general manning · possibly the three largest customers by revenue (§4.3) |
| Principal risk | **Not the market — the bench.** Best managers are already leaving. A unit that cannot staff a turnaround cannot execute one, and a buyer prices thin management directly. Fixable in 30 days and by the board alone (§6.2) |
| Decision rule | **Four kill conditions** (any one fails → exit primary, automatically) and **five scored conditions** (§7). No new business case required to switch |
| Exit alternatives | **Five, ranked**, with partial exit first (§5) |
| Value test | **Net exit value** (full formula, §8.1) compared against **NPV of continuing** including the cash cost of funding further losses and the option value of the turnaround (§8.2). Neither number means anything alone |
| Cost of the plan | Diagnostic and data build · retention · exit readiness · contract exit and closure provisions. Structure at §6.7; illustrative magnitudes in Annex B |
| Decisions sought | **Four**, §1, at this meeting |

### 0.1 Before anything else: the six manoeuvres that will destroy both outcomes

An organisation told it has one year to produce a profitability number will produce a profitability number. There are six well-worn ways to do that in four quarters which permanently destroy the turnaround *and* the sale value, and each is discovered in diligence:

1. Deferring maintenance and fleet capex.
2. Harvesting the backlog on price — booking volume below contribution to fill the order book.
3. Releasing contract provisions and warranty reserves.
4. Cutting the bid, estimating and technical-authority teams (the second restructuring may already have done this).
5. Stretching payables and squeezing subcontractors, i.e. borrowing from the supply chain that delivers the work.
6. Under-recognising loss-making contract positions and over-recognising unbilled work in progress.

**Board action requested:** each of these six is placed on a monthly one-page exception report to the Audit Chair, with the unit CFO personally attesting. This is not distrust of the unit's leadership; it is the removal of a temptation that the deadline itself creates, and saying so plainly is kinder than leaving people to be judged later for responding rationally to the incentive we set.

---

## 1. The four decisions requested at this meeting

| # | Decision | Why now |
|---|---|---|
| **D1** | **Re-specify the deadline** as a *decision* deadline with an evidence standard, not a *profitability* deadline. Month 12 requires: a proven fully-loaded contribution core, a validated run-rate trajectory, and an exit process capable of signature — not a break-even quarter | Without this, §0.1 happens by default (§2) |
| **D2** | **Appoint one accountable owner** with full P&L authority over the unit, reporting to the Group CEO, with the three-branch incentive at §6.1 approved in the same motion | Every week of dual reporting costs a departure (§6.2) |
| **D3** | **Authorise the dual track and the Day-0 start of exit readiness** — vendor diligence, carve-out P&L, standalone cost model, data room — and approve the disclosure architecture at §6.6 | The calendar, not the analysis, is what kills the exit option (§6.5) |
| **D4** | **Adopt the switching rule at §7 as pre-committed**, and name the Group CFO as adjudicator of the shared-customer economics at §3.5 | Rules agreed before the answer is known are the only rules that hold once it is |

Retention actions at §6.2 need no board decision beyond D2's budget line and should be executed within 30 days of this meeting.

---

## 2. On the instruction as given

The board's words were "one final year to produce a credible path to profitability or exit." Two readings sit inside that sentence and they lead to different companies.

**Reading A — profitability deadline.** The unit must show a better EBIT number by Month 12. Achievable, and achievable dishonestly (§0.1).

**Reading B — decision deadline with an evidence standard.** By Month 12 the board must be able to state, on evidence, which of the five options at §5 it is taking, and be far enough into execution that the option is real.

Reading B is what a board can actually act on, and it is also the reading a buyer, a lender and an auditor will each independently apply. The plan below is built on B. If the board prefers A, the plan still runs — but the exception report at §0.1 becomes the single most important document the Audit Chair receives, and the exit route should be assumed to be worth materially less.

---

## 3. Diagnosis: structural or execution-driven

### 3.1 The primary artifact — a three-year EBIT bridge, and a cash bridge beside it

Nothing else is commissioned until these two exist. Both are buildable in two to three weeks from ledgers the unit already has, and together they answer the board's first question more directly than any interview programme.

**EBIT bridge, Year 0 → Year 3, decomposed into:**

| Component | What a large adverse value means |
|---|---|
| Volume | Demand or share loss — read with Test 8 (win-rate/churn) before calling it structural |
| **Price realisation** | Structural if it appears across all segments; execution if concentrated in particular contracts, years or estimators |
| **Mix** | Structural — the profitable work is shrinking faster than the unprofitable work. This is the single most commonly missed driver |
| Input cost inflation not recovered | Structural if contract form prevents recovery (Test 5); execution if indexation clauses exist and were never invoked |
| Productivity / field utilisation | Execution — and the most tractable line in the bridge |
| **Cost-out actually landed in the run rate** | If the landed figure is materially below the programme's claimed figure, the failure was governance, not strategy |
| One-offs, provisions, contract-position remeasurements | Isolate before any conclusion. Restructuring charges and provision movements routinely mask the underlying trend in both directions |

**Cash bridge, same three years.** For a loss-making industrial-services business the cash view is not a supplement; it is half the decision. A unit losing $X of EBIT may be absorbing $2X of cash or may be cash-neutral, and those are two different boards' patience levels and two different sale prices. Required lines: unbilled work in progress and contract assets by ageing · retentions receivable and their realisability · claims and variations recognised but not agreed with the customer · loss-making contract provisions and their adequacy · maintenance versus growth capex, split · working capital days by service line · intercompany funding drawn.

**Sign test, applied at Week 3.** If EBIT losses are stable but cash absorption is worsening, the reported P&L is flattering and the runway is shorter than the board believes. That single finding, if it appears, moves the exit track to primary immediately and is a kill condition at §7.

### 3.2 Reconstructing the two cost programmes — the interpretive rule, not an answer

The temptation is to infer contribution lost from the fact that EBIT did not move. That inference is circular: if losses are flat, contribution lost *must* equal cost removed by arithmetic, and the resulting "decremental margin" is a restatement of the assumption, not a finding. Worse, it is defeated by its own alternatives — price erosion or unrecovered inflation of similar magnitude would produce exactly the same flat EBIT while the departed revenue carried little contribution at all.

So it must be measured bottom-up, and only after the bridge has isolated price and inflation:

**Measure:** for the revenue that actually left over the period, the fully-loaded contribution those specific contracts and branches were generating in the year before exit. Then compare with cost genuinely removed from the run rate (not announced).

| Contribution lost ÷ cost removed | Reading | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| **Under ~25%** | The cuts were largely genuine overhead. The cost base was fat and is now less so | The loss is then explained by price, mix or inflation. Structural — go to §4 segmentation immediately |
| **~25–45%** | Mixed. Some overhead, some capacity | Both tracks live; scrutinise which capabilities went |
| **Above ~45%** | The cuts removed revenue-generating capacity — supervision, estimating, technical authority, field productivity roles | The unit did not have a cost problem and now has a capability problem it did not have three years ago. **A third cost programme would complete the process.** Rebuild before any exit process, or sell a declining asset at a declining multiple |

Then the qualitative half, which is quick and decisive: list the roles removed. If they were disproportionately supervisors, estimators, technical authorities and planners, the answer above is already known.

### 3.3 The honest signal already in front of the board

Best managers transferring out is not merely a symptom; it is an internal forecast produced by the people with the best information and no incentive to flatter it [J]. It should be read as data about the unit's prospects and, separately, as the binding constraint on any turnaround. Both readings point at §6.2.

### 3.4 Nine tests, thirty days

| # | Test | Method | Structural if… | Execution if… |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Margin dispersion** | Fully-loaded contribution by contract, ranked, comparing like work | Whole distribution under water; best quartile barely breaks even | Wide dispersion on comparable work — someone in the unit already knows how to do this profitably |
| 2 | **Price vs. input index** | Realised price per unit of work, five years, against labour and materials indices | Price tracks below input inflation in every segment | Lag concentrated in specific contracts, years or signatories |
| 3 | **Bid-to-final variance** | Bid margin vs. as-built, by contract, estimator, service line | Variance small; bids were always thin — market price is below cost | Variance large and negative — work won by under-estimating. Fixable, and quickly |
| 4 | **Density economics** | Contribution vs. technician/asset density per geography; locate the breakpoint | No geography clears the threshold | Clear breakpoint with a definable subset above it — **this is the shape of a keepable business** |
| 5 | **Contract form audit** | Every contract above a materiality threshold: fixed vs. cost-plus, indexation, change-order mechanism, term, termination, liability caps, LDs | Losses concentrate in a form the market now demands and the unit cannot price safely | Losses concentrate where change-order and indexation rights exist but are unused; unbilled variations un-pursued |
| 6 | **Prequalification and licence integrity** | Approved-vendor status, certifications, licences, safety qualification scores, per customer and per statutory regime; three-year trend | Status lost for reasons not recoverable (scale, financial-standing tests, insurance capacity) | Status lapsed through administrative neglect — recoverable, and cheaply |
| 7 | **HSE record and trend** | TRIR/LTIFR trend, serious-incident frequency, near-miss reporting rate, regulator interactions, customer audit outcomes | Sector risk profile has shifted beyond the unit's insurable or operable capability | Deterioration tracks the loss of supervisors — a capability symptom, and the fastest-moving destroyer of both order book and exit value |
| 8 | **Win-rate and churn decomposition** | Win rate by bid type and year; renewal rate on recurring contracts; every loss coded: price, capability, delivery failure, prequalification failure, **customer insourcing**, **OEM service-arm encroachment**, customer capex cycle | Losses cluster on insourcing, OEM encroachment or capex cycle — the addressable market is contracting | Losses cluster on price errors, delivery failures or bids not submitted |
| 9 | **Relative cost position** | Cost per productive field hour, overhead as % of direct cost, fleet utilisation, benchmarked against listed comparators and known regional competitors | The unit is structurally 15%+ above best comparable cost at equivalent scale, with no path to scale | Gap is in overhead layers, utilisation or subcontract leakage |

**Two further screens, run in parallel, that decide the exit route rather than the diagnosis:**

- **Asset intensity.** Rental fleet, plant, scaffolding, lifting equipment, workshops, property. Book value, market value, age, utilisation, encumbrance. A capital-light manning business and a fleet-heavy business have different buyers, different floors and, in the downside case, different liquidation values.
- **Long-tail liability screen** (Group General Counsel, with external support): pension and multi-employer scheme exposure, asbestos and environmental, latent-defect and warranty tails, historic HSE claims, open disputes and adjudications, decommissioning and site restoration obligations. In this sector these routinely decide the exit route, and occasionally they mean **no buyer will take the entity at any price** — a finding better discovered in Month 2 than in Month 11.
- **Labour structure.** Collective agreements and their expiry dates, works-council and union consultation obligations, transfer-of-undertakings (TUPE/ARD-equivalent) consequences, redundancy cost curves by jurisdiction. These bound both the turnaround cost curve and the divestment mechanics. Union and works-council representatives should be engaged as parties to the process at the earliest lawful moment, not informed after the fact; the cost of being seen to have concealed this from them exceeds any tactical benefit of doing so.

### 3.5 Group-level customer P&L — and the conflict of interest, named

The unit serves customers who also buy from profitable divisions. Two claims will be made about this, both plausible, both self-serving, and both must be tested independently rather than accepted:

1. *"That unit is not really losing what it appears to lose — it prices low to protect our relationship."* Tends to be **understated** by the divisions receiving the benefit.
2. *"If you sell or close it, we lose material revenue in our division."*
